The town kept its spare time in a building beside the railway station.

It was not a bank, although newcomers often mistook it for one. There were brass handles on the doors and a clock above the entrance, but the clock had no hands. Inside, a woman named Ada sat behind a wooden counter, accepting minutes.

People brought them in all sorts of containers.

A schoolboy arrived with eleven minutes in a jam jar: the remainder of a canceled spelling test. A doctor deposited half an hour that had opened unexpectedly between appointments. Once, a man carried in three entire days wrapped in a blanket. He had been stood up at the altar and did not want to discuss it.

Ada issued receipts.

“What happens to it?” the schoolboy asked.

“It keeps.”

“Does it go bad?”

“Only if you spend too long wishing it were a different kind.”

He looked at his jar. The minutes inside moved like small fish.

“Can I have it back?”

“Of course.”

“Not yet,” he said, and pushed it toward her.

***

There were rules.

You could deposit only time you had genuinely been given. You could not bring the hours you stole from sleep, or the afternoon you spent avoiding a difficult conversation. Ada turned away many such offerings.

“This isn’t spare,” she would say gently. “You owe it to someone.”

You could withdraw your own time whenever you liked.

You could also donate it.

The donation shelf stood behind the counter, beside a fern that had been green for sixty years.

Most donations were small: five minutes, a quarter of an hour. People left them without ceremony. A tired mother. A delivery driver. An old woman who said she had more Tuesdays than she needed.

Ada never asked why.

***

One November evening, a girl came in carrying nothing.

She was perhaps seventeen, though worry had made a poor job of counting her years.

“My father,” she said.

Ada waited.

“The hospital says tonight.”

Outside, a train passed without stopping. The glasses on the shelves gave a faint, bright shiver.

“How much do you need?” Ada asked.

“I don’t know.”

“That’s usual.”

“Does it make people well?”

“No.”

The girl looked down.

Ada brought a small blue cup from the donation shelf.

“What does it do, then?”

“It gives you time.”

The girl stared at the cup for a long while. Then she took it carefully in both hands.

***

Afterward, she came back.

It was morning. Rain had darkened the shoulders of her coat.

“Did you use it?” Ada asked.

“Yes.”

The girl set the empty cup on the counter.

“Was it enough?”

“No.”

Ada nodded.

“But he told me where he put the seeds,” the girl said. “For the garden. I thought they were in the shed, but he said mice would get them there. They’re in an old biscuit tin above the fridge.”

She touched the handle of the cup.

“He made me promise not to plant all the beans at once.”

Ada reached for a cloth and dried a little rain from the counter.

“I wrote it down,” the girl said.

***

Ada had worked at the building for forty-three years.

She had inherited the position from a man called Mr. Vale, who had explained the ledgers, the shelves, the difference between a moment and a minute.

“A moment,” he had said, “doesn’t fit reliably into anything.”

On her first day, Ada had asked whether employees received an allowance.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“You’ll be tempted to take some anyway.”

She had been twenty-six then, and disliked him for saying it.

Now she was sixty-nine. In her handbag she carried a receipt dated the year before she began work: forty minutes from a train delay.

She had been saving them for something.

For years she had imagined an emergency. Then a journey. Then an afternoon with her sister, who lived by the sea and kept asking her to visit.

Her sister had died in March.

The receipt remained.

***

On the first warm day of spring, Ada put a sign on the door.

BACK IN FORTY MINUTES.

She took her deposit in a plain glass bottle and walked to the park.

A groundskeeper was repairing a bench. Two children argued over a bicycle. Beside the pond, a young man rehearsed something under his breath, stopped, and began again.

Ada found a dry place on the grass.

For a while she held the bottle between her knees. She had forgotten to bring a book. At work, there were cups to wash and a ledger waiting for its new page.

She loosened the stopper.

A dog came over and inspected her shoes. Its owner apologized. Ada said it was all right.

When the woman had gone, Ada lay back, awkwardly, with her handbag beneath her head.

Above her, among the new leaves, a bird was pulling at a length of string caught on a branch.

Ada watched until it came free.
